questions.body: When `box-sizing: border-box` is set on an element, what components are included within its specified `width` and `height`?
questions.keyPoints: Content, padding, and border are included; margin remains outside.

options.text: Content, padding, and border (margins are excluded).
options.explanation: With `border-box`, `width = content + padding + border`. Margins remain outside the box dimensions. In `content-box` (default), padding and border add to the specified width.

options.text: Content only.
options.explanation: That describes the default `content-box`.

options.text: Content, padding, border, and margin.
options.explanation: Margin is never included within element width.

options.text: Padding and margin only.
options.explanation: Content and border are fundamental box model layers.

questions.body: In a flex container with default `flex-direction: row`, which property controls alignment along the cross (vertical) axis?
questions.keyPoints: justify-content aligns on main axis; align-items aligns on cross axis.

options.text: `align-items`
options.explanation: In `flex-direction: row`, the main axis is horizontal and controlled by `justify-content`. The cross axis is vertical and controlled by `align-items` (or `align-self` for individual items).

options.text: `justify-content`
options.explanation: `justify-content` aligns along the main axis.

options.text: `flex-align`
options.explanation: `flex-align` is not a standard CSS property.

options.text: `vertical-align`
options.explanation: `vertical-align` applies to inline and table-cell elements, not flex containers.

questions.body: What do the three values in `flex: 1 0 200px` represent in order?
questions.keyPoints: flex-grow, flex-shrink, flex-basis.

options.text: `flex-grow`, `flex-shrink`, and `flex-basis`
options.explanation: The `flex` shorthand syntax is `flex: <flex-grow> <flex-shrink> <flex-basis>`. In this example, it can grow with factor 1, cannot shrink (0), and has initial basis of 200px.

options.text: `flex-shrink`, `flex-grow`, and `flex-order`
options.explanation: Grow comes first, shrink second.

options.text: `flex-basis`, `flex-grow`, and `flex-shrink`
options.explanation: Basis is the third value.

options.text: `flex-direction`, `flex-wrap`, and `flex-gap`
options.explanation: Those are container properties, not item flex sizing shorthand.

questions.body: In CSS Grid, what does `grid-template-columns: 1fr 2fr` do?
questions.keyPoints: Divides available free space into 3 parts, allocating 1/3 to the first column and 2/3 to the second.

options.text: It divides available free space into 3 fractional parts, giving 1 part to column 1 and 2 parts to column 2.
options.explanation: The `fr` (fractional) unit distributes available free space proportionally after fixed items and gaps are accounted for.

options.text: It fixes column 1 to 100px and column 2 to 200px.
options.explanation: `fr` is dynamic fractional space, not fixed pixels.

options.text: It sets column 1 to 1 frame rate (16ms) and column 2 to 2 frame rates.
options.explanation: `fr` means fraction, not animation frame.

options.text: It scales columns relative to screen DPI ratio.
options.explanation: It partitions grid track space.

questions.body:
Rank the following selectors from lowest to highest specificity:
1. `.btn.active`
2. `#nav`
3. `nav li a`
4. `style="color: red"` (inline)
questions.keyPoints: Element (0,0,1) < Class (0,2,0) < ID (1,0,0) < Inline style (1,0,0,0).

options.text: `nav li a` (0,0,3) < `.btn.active` (0,2,0) < `#nav` (1,0,0) < Inline style
options.explanation: Specificity is evaluated in columns: Inline (1000) > ID (100) > Class/Attribute/Pseudo-class (10) > Type/Pseudo-element (1). Hence 3 < 1 < 2 < 4.

options.text: `.btn.active` < `nav li a` < `#nav` < Inline style
options.explanation: Classes have higher specificity weight than element type selectors.

options.text: `#nav` < `.btn.active` < `nav li a` < Inline style
options.explanation: ID selectors outweigh classes.

options.text: All four have equal specificity because order of appearance decides.
options.explanation: Order of appearance only breaks ties when specificities are identical.

questions.body: What is the primary benefit of CSS Cascade Layers (`@layer`)?
questions.keyPoints: Explicitly controls cascade order between layers regardless of selector specificity within them.

options.text: It allows developers to explicitly control the priority order of style sources (e.g. reset, framework, utilities) regardless of selector specificity within those layers.
options.explanation: `@layer` rules establish a clear cascade priority order. Styles in higher-priority layers always win over lower layers, even if a selector in a lower layer has higher specificity.

options.text: It converts 2D CSS layouts into 3D WebGL canvases.
options.explanation: `@layer` is purely an architecture feature of the CSS cascade.

options.text: It replaces media queries for mobile responsiveness.
options.explanation: Media queries are unaffected; `@layer` organizes cascade specificity.

options.text: It automatically purges unused CSS classes during Webpack builds.
options.explanation: It is a native browser runtime CSS standard.

questions.body: What does `position: absolute` position an element relative to?
questions.keyPoints: Its nearest positioned ancestor (ancestor with position other than static), or initial containing block.

options.text: Its closest ancestor element that has a `position` other than `static` (or the viewport/initial containing block if none exists).
options.explanation: `position: absolute` removes the element from normal document flow and positions it relative to the nearest ancestor with `position: relative`, `absolute`, `fixed`, or `sticky`.

options.text: Always the browser viewport window.
options.explanation: Positioning relative to the viewport is the behavior of `position: fixed`.

options.text: Its immediate parent element regardless of its parent's CSS position.
options.explanation: If the immediate parent is `position: static`, it traverses further up.

options.text: The center of the document body.
options.explanation: It uses top/right/bottom/left offsets relative to the positioned containing block.

questions.body: Under what condition will `position: sticky` fail to stick while scrolling?
questions.keyPoints: If an ancestor has overflow: hidden, scroll, or auto, or if top/bottom offset is omitted.

options.text: If an ancestor element has `overflow: hidden`, `overflow: auto`, or `overflow: scroll`, or if no offset (`top`, `bottom`) is specified.
options.explanation: `position: sticky` requires a threshold offset (like `top: 0`) and will be constrained by any scrollable or clipping parent ancestor that creates an overflow boundary.

options.text: If the element contains text longer than 100 characters.
options.explanation: Text length does not affect sticky positioning.

options.text: If JavaScript is disabled in the browser.
options.explanation: `position: sticky` is purely declarative CSS, requiring zero JavaScript.

options.text: If the parent element has `display: flex`.
options.explanation: Sticky elements work inside flex containers as long as the container has sufficient height to scroll within.

questions.body: What does `grid-template-columns: subgrid` allow a nested grid item to do?
questions.keyPoints: Allows a child grid to inherit and align with the track sizing of its parent grid.

options.text: It allows a nested child element to inherit and directly align its own items with the grid lines and track sizing of its parent grid.
options.explanation: `subgrid` enables child components to participate in the row/column track definitions of the parent grid, aligning nested items without having to declare matching track sizes manually.

options.text: It creates a nested Flexbox container inside each grid cell.
options.explanation: It shares grid lines, not Flexbox.

options.text: It duplicates the parent DOM structure.
options.explanation: It is purely CSS track inheritance.

options.text: It forces all nested columns to be 100px wide.
options.explanation: It adopts whatever track sizing the parent grid uses.

questions.body: Which HTML5 element represents self-contained content that could be independently distributable or reusable (e.g., a blog post, forum reply, or product card)?
questions.keyPoints: <article> represents an independent self-contained composition.

options.text: `<article>`
options.explanation: `<article>` is intended for self-contained, independently syndicatable content. `<section>` groups related thematic content. `<aside>` represents tangential content (sidebars).

options.text: `<section>`
options.explanation: `<section>` represents a thematic grouping of content, typically with a heading.

options.text: `<aside>`
options.explanation: `<aside>` represents content indirectly related to main content like sidebars or pull quotes.

options.text: `<div>`
options.explanation: `<div>` has zero semantic meaning; it is purely a generic styling container.

questions.body: When two adjacent vertical block margins touch (e.g., top element `margin-bottom: 30px` and bottom element `margin-top: 20px`), what is the resulting space between them in normal flow?
questions.keyPoints: Vertical margins collapse to the maximum of the two margins.

options.text: `30px` (they collapse to the maximum of the adjoining margins).
options.explanation: In standard block flow, vertical margins of adjacent sibling boxes collapse into a single margin whose size is the largest of the two margins.

options.text: `50px` (the sum of the two margins).
options.explanation: Horizontal margins add up, but vertical block margins collapse.

options.text: `20px` (the minimum of the two margins).
options.explanation: Margin collapse takes the maximum positive margin.

options.text: `10px` (the difference between the two margins).
options.explanation: Margins do not subtract unless one is negative.

questions.body: Which of the following CSS declarations triggers the creation of a new Block Formatting Context (BFC) on an element?
questions.keyPoints: overflow: hidden/auto, display: flow-root, flex, grid, inline-block create BFC.

options.text: `display: flow-root;` or `overflow: hidden;`
options.explanation: `display: flow-root` explicitly creates a new BFC without side effects, containing internal floats and preventing external margin collapsing. `overflow: hidden` also establishes a BFC.

options.text: `position: static;`
options.explanation: Static position does not create a BFC.

options.text: `display: inline;`
options.explanation: Inline elements participate in an Inline Formatting Context, not BFC.

options.text: `margin: auto;`
options.explanation: Margin centering does not establish formatting contexts.

questions.body: How do CSS Custom Properties (e.g., `--primary-color: #3b82f6;`) differ from preprocessor variables (Sass/Less)?
questions.keyPoints: CSS custom properties are dynamic at runtime, inherit through the DOM, and can be manipulated via JS.

options.text: They are live and dynamic in the browser runtime, cascade down the DOM hierarchy, and can be read or modified by JavaScript at runtime.
options.explanation: Sass variables compile down to static values at build time. Native CSS variables (`var(--name)`) are reactive, inherit along the DOM tree, and can change dynamically via classes, media queries, or JS.

options.text: They only work inside SVGs.
options.explanation: They work across all CSS properties and HTML elements.

options.text: They cannot have fallback values.
options.explanation: Fallbacks are supported: `var(--color, #000)`.

options.text: They must be compiled using Node.js before browsers can parse them.
options.explanation: They are native CSS supported in all modern browsers.

questions.body: What problem do CSS Container Queries (`@container`) solve that Media Queries (`@media`) cannot?
questions.keyPoints: Container queries style components based on the size of their parent container rather than the viewport.

options.text: They allow components to adapt styles based on the width/height of their parent container rather than the overall browser viewport.
options.explanation: A component in a narrow sidebar versus wide main column can adjust its internal layout based on `@container (min-width: 400px)`, making design truly modular and reusable.

options.text: They query the user's available GPU memory.
options.explanation: They query layout dimensions of ancestor container elements.

options.text: They enable styling based on user screen orientation only.
options.explanation: Media queries already handle screen orientation.

options.text: They automatically bundle CSS into Docker containers.
options.explanation: Container queries refer to DOM layout containers, not server containers.

questions.body: What is the key specificity difference between the CSS `:is()` and `:where()` pseudo-classes?
questions.keyPoints: :is() takes the specificity of its most specific argument; :where() always has 0 specificity.

options.text: `:is()` adopts the specificity of its most specific selector argument, while `:where()` always has a specificity score of zero (`0, 0, 0`).
options.explanation: Both accept selector lists for grouping (e.g. `header, main, footer p`), but `:where(...)` has 0 specificity making styles easy to override in design systems.

options.text: `:where()` only works with ID selectors.
options.explanation: Both accept any valid selector list.

options.text: `:is()` has been deprecated in favor of `:has()`.
options.explanation: All three are active modern W3C standards with distinct purposes.

options.text: `:where()` executes asynchronously via MutationObserver.
options.explanation: They are standard CSS selector matching functions.

questions.body: What does the selector `article:has(img)` target?
questions.keyPoints: :has() is the CSS parent selector targeting elements that contain matching descendants.

options.text:
Any `
` element that contains at least one `` descendant.
options.explanation: `:has()` functions as a relational 'parent selector', styling an element based on descendants or subsequent siblings matching the relative selector.

options.text:
Only `` elements that are children of an `
`.
options.explanation: That would be `article img`.

options.text: Articles that do NOT have any image elements.
options.explanation: That would be `article:not(:has(img))`.

options.text: All images inside the entire document.
options.explanation: It targets `<article>` elements conditionally.

questions.body: What is the difference between `` and the `` element?
questions.keyPoints: srcset lets the browser pick the best resolution/size; picture is for art direction and format switching.

options.text: `srcset` allows the browser to choose the most optimal image based on device pixel density and layout width; `<picture>` is used for art direction (different image crops per breakpoint) or format fallback (AVIF/WebP/PNG).
options.explanation: `srcset` gives the browser options to serve resolution-matched files. `<picture>` gives the developer explicit control to dictate different image crops or formats via `<source media="..." type="...">`.

options.text: `<picture>` only works on mobile devices.
options.explanation: Both work across all responsive viewport sizes.

options.text: `srcset` requires JavaScript to select the image source.
options.explanation: The browser pre-parser handles `srcset` natively before JS executes.

options.text: `` does not support an `` fallback tag.
options.explanation: A `` element must contain an `` element inside as the rendered fallback.

questions.body: What performance optimization does `contain: content;` or `contain: strict;` offer to browser rendering engines?
questions.keyPoints: Isolates the element subtree so changes inside do not trigger reflows or repaints outside it.

options.text: It informs the browser that the element's subtree is isolated from the rest of the page, preventing style, layout, and paint recalculations from propagating outside.
options.explanation: CSS containment tells the engine that an element's internal layout/paint changes will not affect outside elements, allowing the browser to skip calculating layout for outside nodes during updates.

options.text: It restricts the element from making HTTP network requests.
options.explanation: That is Content Security Policy (CSP), not CSS containment.

options.text: It hides the element entirely from the DOM tree.
options.explanation: That would be `display: none`.

options.text: It limits maximum memory usage to 10 MB.
options.explanation: Containment optimizes rendering pipeline recalculations.

questions.body: What is the primary rule regarding the use of ARIA attributes in HTML?
questions.keyPoints: First Rule of ARIA: Do not use ARIA if a native HTML element or attribute exists.

options.text: The First Rule of ARIA: If you can use a native HTML element (e.g. `<button>`, `<input>`) with the required semantics, do not use ARIA attributes instead.
options.explanation: Native HTML elements come with built-in accessibility semantics, focusability, and keyboard interactions (Enter/Space on buttons) that ARIA attributes do not automatically provide.

options.text: Every single HTML tag must have an `aria-label` attribute.
options.explanation: Overusing ARIA labels can clutter assistive tech and introduce bugs.

options.text: ARIA attributes override and disable standard CSS styling.
options.explanation: ARIA does not interfere with CSS rendering.

options.text: ARIA is only used for search engine SEO bots.
options.explanation: ARIA is specifically for assistive technologies like screen readers.

questions.body: Why should images and iframes always specify explicit `width` and `height` attributes in HTML?
questions.keyPoints: Allows the browser to calculate aspect ratio and reserve layout space, preventing Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS).

options.text: It enables the browser to calculate the aspect ratio and reserve the required layout space before the image file finishes downloading, eliminating Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS).
options.explanation: With `width` and `height` attributes present, modern browsers calculate `aspect-ratio` automatically. The space is reserved in layout, preventing content from jarringly jumping when images load.

options.text: Without them, the browser will refuse to load images over HTTPS.
options.explanation: Images load regardless, but with layout shifts.

options.text: It forces image compression on the server side.
options.explanation: HTML attributes do not affect server file compression.

options.text: It prevents users from right-clicking to save the image.
options.explanation: Does not affect context menu behavior.
